extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetry, drama, and literary criticism; poets and dramatists studying Aristotelian poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing and judging poetry and tragedy according to Aristotelian poetics: emphasis on mimesis, unity, plot, character, diction, catharsis, and the aims of art. Useful for critics, playwrights, and students of literary theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis) as the common principle
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Imitation’ (μίμησις) is the common principle of the arts of poetry, music, dancing, painting, and sculpture; arts differ according to medium, objects, and manner of imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works by how they enact mimesis: identify the medium (rhythm, language, harmony), the objects imitated (types of people/actions), and the manner (narration vs dramatic presentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation (rhythm, language, harmony)
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium of imitation is rhythm, language, and ‘harmony’ (or melody), taken singly or combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the chosen medium (e.g., metre, melody, rhetoric) is appropriate and effectively employed for the poem's aims; e.g., tragedy uses a combination, dance relies on rhythm alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation (higher or lower types)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects of imitation are men in action, represented as better, worse, or as they are—this distinction underlies differences like Tragedy (better) and Comedy (worse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the moral/typological framing of characters (nobler than life, truer to life, or inferior) and whether that choice suits the genre and thematic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation (dramatic presentation vs narration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may imitate by narration (authorial voice) or by showing characters living and moving before us (drama); forms include dramatic narrative, pure narrative (including lyric), or pure drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate if the chosen manner (narration vs dramatization) is consistent and effective for achieving the intended universality and emotional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic Truth vs Historical (empirical) Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is not a reproduction of empirical fact: the ‘probabilities’ and ‘possibilities’ of Poetry contrasted with those of experience; Poetry represents the universal through the particular and excludes the rule of Chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess poetic truth by its internal necessity, probability, and capacity to express the universal — not by literal factual accuracy; check adherence to 'probable or necessary sequence' among incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poem as an organism / Ideal unity of Poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception of a poem as an organism: ideal unity of Poetry; the plot must be a Whole, complete in itself, and of adequate magnitude; beginning, middle, and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate structural unity: whether parts are organically connected and the whole achieves coherence and proportionality (adequate magnitude, clear beginning/middle/end).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (primary dramatic unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Action is the primary Unity: unity of plot consists not in Unity of Hero, but in Unity of Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize whether the work maintains a single, causally coherent action; avoid extraneous subplots that break the unity of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Time and Unity of Place (minor unities)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Unity of Time’: the practice of the Greek stage; ‘Unity of Place’ is nowhere mentioned in Aristotle; the higher law of ‘Unity of Action’ often subordinates the minor unities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider time/place constraints as secondary rules: they may be observed for effect but should not override the unity of action or organic integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six elements of Tragedy (evaluation dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Six elements in Tragedy: Spectacular Presentment (ὁ τῆς ὄψεως κόσμος or σκηνή), Lyrical Song (μελοποιία), Diction (λέξις), Plot (μῦθος), Character (ἤθος), and Thought (διάνοια). Plot is of primary importance; Character and Thought come next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these six elements as explicit axes for critique: judge spectacle, music, language, plot construction, moral portrayal, and intellectual content, with special weight on plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must be a Whole and of adequate magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot must be a Whole, complete in itself, and of adequate magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the plot is complete, proportionate, and sufficiently developed to produce the intended tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of probable or necessary sequence in incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic Unity can be attained only by the observance of Poetic as distinct from Historic Truth; the rule of probable or necessary sequence as applied to the incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate causal logic: incidents should follow by probability or necessity, not by chance, to sustain poetic truth and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of the Inevitable and the Unexpected
rubrics_metrics.description: The best Tragic effects depend on the combination of the Inevitable and the Unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge plot reversals and surprises for whether they feel both necessary and surprising, contributing to catharsis rather than undermining plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs Simple plots; Peripeteia and Recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of Simple (ἁπλοῖ) and Complex (πεπλεγμένοι) Plots; Reversal of the Situation (περιπέτεια), Recognition (ἀναγνώρισις), and Tragic or disastrous Incident (πάθος) defined and explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the plot uses reversal and recognition effectively (complex plot) or is simple; evaluate how these mechanisms generate pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts of Tragedy (prologue, episode, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘quantitative parts’ (μέρη κατὰ τὸ ποσόν) of Tragedy defined — Prologue, Episode, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine structure in terms of traditional parts and whether their ordering and length serve the whole; beware interpolations or misplaced parts that disrupt unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic emotions should spring from Plot, not Spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic emotions of pity and fear should spring out of the Plot itself; to produce them by Scenery or Spectacular effect is entirely against the spirit of Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique emotional effects: they must be motivated by events and character, not manufactured by spectacle or cheap theatrical tricks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as manifestation of moral purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of Character (as the manifestation of moral purpose) in Tragedy; requisites of ethical portraiture; rule of necessity or probability applicable to Character as to Plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate characters for coherent moral purpose, credible motivations, and actions that follow necessity or probability; avoid characters whose actions are inexplicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal tragic hero and hamartia
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal type of protagonist is deduced from the function of Tragedy to produce pity and fear; Aristotle’s ideal protagonist and the meaning of ἁμαρτία (hamartia); excluded character types (blameless goodness, signal villainy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the protagonist: they should be 'spoudaios' (serious) with a fall arising from a flaw or error that elicits pity and fear, not mere virtue or pure villainy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Deus ex Machina
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘Deus ex Machina’ is criticised (a passage out of place) — an intervention out of place is inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge resolutions: avoid contrived or external devices that resolve the action without organic cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical craft rules for the tragic poet
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rules: (1) To place the scene before his eyes, and to act the parts himself to enter into vivid sympathy with the dramatis personae; (2) To sketch the bare outline of the action before proceeding to fill in the episodes; (3) To be careful about the Complication (δέσις) and Dénouement (λύσις); (4) To unite, if possible, varied forms of poetic excellence; (5) Not to overcharge a Tragedy with details appropriate to Epic Poetry; (6) To make the Choral Odes—like the Dialogue—an organic part of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these as prescriptive craft checks when composing: ensure embodied empathy for characters, plan outlines first, manage complication and denouement carefully, balance elements, avoid epic over-detail, and integrate chorus/odes organically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (διάνοια) and Diction (λέξις)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (διάνοια), or the intellectual element, is revealed in dramatic speeches composed according to the rules of Rhetoric. Diction falls largely within the domain of the Art of Delivery rather than of Poetry. Poetic Diction includes Metaphor; how Poetry combines elevation of language with perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the intellectual content and persuasive reasoning of speeches, and appraise language for elevated expression that remains clear; examine use of metaphor and appropriate modes of speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's aim: pleasure and higher enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of Fine Art is pleasure. Its lower forms afford the pleasure of a pastime (παιδιά); its higher forms, that noble enjoyment which belongs to supreme happiness (εὐδαιμονία). The pleasure of the hearer or spectator (θεατής) is the end of Art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate aesthetic effect by the quality of pleasure produced: distinguish mere pastime from noble enjoyment; consider whether the work advances the spectator’s intellectual or emotional satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgment primary over didactic/moral function
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle distinguishes the educational from the aesthetic function of Poetry: his critical estimates of Poetry rest on purely aesthetic grounds; yet some rules indicate a sense of ethical excellence (e.g., tragic characters must be σπουδαῖοι).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize aesthetic criteria when judging poetic quality, while recognizing that moral character and ethical portraiture can affect aesthetic evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs Tragedy: shared unity and distinguishing features
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic Poetry agrees with Tragedy in Unity of Action; points of difference include (1) length of the poem, (2) the metre, (3) the art of imparting a plausible air to incredible fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating epic, check for unified action on a larger scale and for strategies that render vast or incredible material plausibly; consider metre and length as genre-appropriate devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry’s psychological and historical origins (imitation, rhythm, harmony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychologically, Poetry may be traced to two causes: the instinct of Imitation, and the instinct of ‘Harmony’ and ‘Rhythm’. Historically, poetry diverged early into forms (tragedy/comedy) reflecting these tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how a work exploits innate human pleasures in imitation and rhythmic/harmonic forms; craft that aligns with these instincts will more readily engage audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of spectacle and musical elements (external elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacular Presentment (scene/visuals), Lyrical Song, and Diction are external elements of tragedy; spectacle is less important than plot for producing true tragic emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate spectacle and music as supporting elements that should be subordinate to plot and character; excessive reliance on spectacle to produce emotion is a flaw.
